The fluorescent lights of the 14th floor hummed with the same energy as the panic rising in Dave’s throat. It was "Bring Your Pet to Work Day," a corporate initiative that Dave had interpreted as "Bring Your Emotional Support Animal to Work Day," but his boss, Mr. Henderson, had interpreted it as "Bring Your Dog to Work Day."

Dave’s pet, Barnaby, was a African Grey Parrot with a vocabulary that ranged from "Pretty Bird" to "I know where the bodies are buried," mostly because Dave had spent the last three years rehearsing his quarterly earnings calls in the living room while Barnaby watched.

"Dave," Mr. Henderson said, leaning over Dave’s cubicle wall, his coffee mug hovering dangerously close to Barnaby’s cage. "Why is your parrot wearing a tie?"

"It’s... it’s a fashion statement," Dave squeaked. "Very trendy in the Amazon."

Barnaby tilted his head, fixed his beady eye on Henderson, and squawked, "Quarterly projections are down! We’re cooking the books! Also, Dave, you’re out of milk!"

The office went silent. The only sound was the hum of the fluorescent lights and the distant clacking of keyboards from the accounting department, who were probably already typing up their resignation letters.

Henderson blinked. "Dave. Did your bird just admit to cooking the books?"

"No! No, sir! He’s... he’s an actor! Method acting! He’s preparing for a role in *The Wolf of Wall Street*!" Dave stood up, knocking his chair over. "Barnaby, hush! Bad bird! No insider trading!"

Barnaby, sensing the drama, flapped his wings and shouted, "Henderson’s wife knows about the golf trips! She knows! She knows!"

Henderson’s face turned the color of a ripe tomato. "Dave! Get that bird out of here!"

"But sir, it’s against company policy to remove pets before 3 PM!" Dave yelled, trying to cover the cage with a stack of confidential files.

"Policy? POLICY?!" Henderson roared. "That bird just leaked my marital secrets and our fiscal irresponsibility in the same breath! Get him out! Now!"
